summary: Norway's data protection authority, Datatilsynet, has asked the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) to make its emergency ban on Meta's consentless tracking and profiling for ad targeting permanent and EU-wide. The local ban, issued in July under GDPR urgency powers, carries a daily fine of up to one million NOK, which Meta has ignored while a court rejected its injunction bid. Meta says it will move to consent as its legal basis but has given no date, so the referral could force the change sooner.
one_line: Norway's data protection authority asks the EDPB to extend its ban on Meta's consentless tracking ads across the EU single market.
key_facts: Norway's data protection authority, Datatilsynet, asked the EDPB to take a binding decision on making its emergency ban on Meta's tracking and profiling for ads permanent and EU-wide.
Datatilsynet issued its local ban on Meta tracking and profiling users without consent in July, using GDPR powers that allow temporary measures lasting three months.
The Datatilsynet order includes a daily fine of up to one million NOK (~$100,000) per day for non-compliance, and Meta has continued to ignore it.
Meta sought a court injunction against the order, but an Oslo court rejected its arguments earlier in September 2023, affirming the DPA's right to act.
Meta's lead GDPR regulator is the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC); the Norwegian emergency action circumvents the 'one-stop-shop' mechanism.
The EDPB Secretariat will assess completeness of the file; once done, the art. 66(4) GDPR deadline starts and the Board has two weeks to adopt its urgent binding decision.
The EDPB declined to say how long its completeness assessment will take.
Late in 2022 the EDPB settled a dispute between DPAs on Meta's legal basis for ads, leading in January to a DPC decision rejecting Meta's claim of contractual necessity.
In July the EU's top court ruled, in a case brought by Germany's competition authority, that Meta cannot claim legitimate interest to run 'personalized ads' without user consent.
At the start of August Meta announced an 'intention' to ask users for permission for its tracking ads, but has not done so or announced a date.
Meta spokesperson Matt Pollard said Meta was surprised by the NDPA's actions, is in discussions via the Irish DPC, and said 'We have not announced a date.'
